component.name: FujiNet Go Intv
component.summary: Self-contained Mattel Intellivision with built-in FujiNet

description.p: A Mattel Intellivision with FujiNet built in: boots straight into FujiNet's config ROM, with a clickable keypad window standing in for both hand controllers so every keypad button and direction disc can be driven with a mouse.

Emulation is provided by a FujiNet-patched jzIntv, with FujiNet attached over Bus-Over-IP (BoIP) on loopback TCP. The debugger covers the CP-1610 CPU and the STIC graphics chip -- registers, mode, the BACKTAB background grid, the 8 MOBs (sprites), and the GRAM/GROM card sheet. Plain Qt6 Widgets, not KDE Frameworks -- Breeze arrives through the platform theme.

The bundled FujiNet runtime moves back onto upstream master. The previous build came from a branch that was never merged, so it had been sitting still while upstream moved on; this picks up the device-chain rework and the Drivewire cassette media format along with the merged Mbed TLS 3.x requirement it was branched for.

The bundled FujiNet runtime moves to a firmware build that refuses to compile against Mbed TLS 4.x. That release removed the low-level crypto headers the runtime's TLS backend needs and split the rest into a separate library, so a machine whose system Mbed TLS had moved to 4.x could produce a build with broken TLS instead of a clear failure. The build now finds a 3.x install, or stops and says so.
It also picks up Gmail message composition, and the calendar protocols gain the ability to create and edit events rather than only read them.

The bundled FujiNet runtime gains calendars. Programs running on the emulated Intellivision can now open CALENDAR, GCAL (Google Calendar) and ICAL (iCalendar over HTTP) network URLs the same way they already open Google Drive and Gmail, and read the events back as plain text.

Fixed the violent flicker in the embedded FujiNet CONFIG menu. Every screen with a selection bar redrew its whole list each time the bar moved, which was far more work than one video frame allows, so the list was visibly seen repainting in pieces. Moving the selection now touches only the two rows that change, and the network list no longer re-fetches every SSID to do it.

The embedded FujiNet CONFIG menu is now in colour throughout. Host slots, the network info screen, the file browser, the character keyboard and the boot screen each have their own palette, the file browser marks folders and cartridges with icons, and the keyboard highlights the selected key in inverse video.

The Linux .deb/.rpm/.tar.gz packages built a shared libSDL3 instead of linking it statically, so they depended on a system libSDL3.so no distribution actually ships. SDL3 is now statically linked into the Linux packages, matching the Windows and macOS builds.

There was no way to restart the game you were playing short of reloading it from FujiNet CONFIG, and no keyboard shortcut back to CONFIG itself -- only a menu item and Ctrl+R, unreachable from a gamepad and unable to be remapped to a different key.

Backspace now soft-resets the running game in place, the way a real Intellivision's own RESET switch does: the cartridge stays mapped and FujiNet stays connected, so a game pushed over the network restarts as itself instead of dropping back to CONFIG. Escape returns to CONFIG, reachable by keypress now as well as the menu. Both are new buttons in the keypad window's own row and, like every keypad button and disc segment, can be rebound to any key or gamepad button through Map mode.

The keypad window's Map button could rebind any digit or action button but not the direction disc itself: the disc's sixteen positions stayed on their fixed keyboard/stick/D-pad bindings no matter what, so a gamepad had no way to reach the eight half-step positions between the compass directions, and a keyboard layout that didn't suit a given game or player couldn't be changed there either.

Map mode now covers all sixteen disc segments on both controllers, the same way it already covers the fifteen digit and action buttons: click Map, click a sector of the disc, then press whichever keyboard key or gamepad button should drive it. The armed sector lights up amber, separate from the blue wedge that shows the disc's live position, and the status line and Reset Bindings work exactly as they already did for keypad buttons.

On Windows, the keypad window's Map button could bind a gamepad button but never a keyboard key: arm Map, click a keypad button, press a key, and nothing happened -- worse, pressing Space or Enter cancelled the whole mapping instead. Windows delivers a keystroke only to whichever control currently holds keyboard focus, and clicking Map left focus sitting on the Map button itself, where nothing was listening for it. Gamepad capture worked regardless, since it's polled rather than focus-driven, which is why only the keyboard half was ever affected.

Keyboard mapping now works the same as it always has on the other three frontends. The identical bug affected the ECS keyboard window's on-screen Ctrl and Shift buttons, fixed the same way: physical typing no longer goes silent after clicking either one.

The keypad window's buttons and disc were fixed in place: a keyboard layout that didn't match Mattel's original 1979 numpad assignment had no way to be changed, and a physical gamepad had no access to the numeric keypad at all -- only the disc and three action buttons.

A Map button in the keypad window fixes both. Click Map, click any of the fifteen digit or action buttons on either controller, then press whichever keyboard key or gamepad button should drive it. The window shows what it's currently bound to and confirms the new binding once made, saying what it took the input from if that input was already in use elsewhere. Reset Bindings restores every default at once. Mappings are shared across all four frontends and saved between sessions.

Some cartridges refused to load from FujiNet at all, stopping on the boot screen with "TRUNCATED XFER". These were the larger homebrew titles -- Cloudfire, frantic 4 and Pacmanthology among them -- which describe their memory layout in far more detail than an original Intellivision cartridge does, use bank switching to reach past the console's address space, and add the JLP expansion for extra memory and save games.

The loader that handled cartridges arriving over FujiNet was a simplified one and understood none of that. It now hands them to the emulator's own cartridge loader instead -- the same one used when you open a game from disk -- so a game pushed from FujiNet and the same game opened locally now behave identically. Save games for JLP titles are kept per title and survive between sessions.

The boot progress bar now tracks the actual transfer. It had been measuring against a fixed guess rather than the cartridge's real size, so a small cartridge crawled part-way across and then jumped to the end, while a large one filled the bar within the first few seconds and sat there for the rest of the transfer.

Larger cartridges loaded from FujiNet came up corrupted. The transfer itself completed and the game started, but its graphics and code were subtly wrong -- most of the 32K and 48K Intellivision-era titles were affected, since nearly all of them share the same memory layout.

When a pushed cartridge replaced the FujiNet boot menu, the boot menu's own memory stayed mapped alongside the new game's rather than being released, and the console ended up reading both at once. Where the two overlapped, half of every value the game read was quietly lost. The outgoing cartridge is now unmapped before the new one takes its place.

Booting a cartridge from FujiNet could stop dead partway through the transfer, leaving the console on the "BOOTING / DO NOT POWER OFF" screen with the progress bar frozen and the title line drawn as garbage. Whether a title was affected came down to its own data: roughly half the 32K Intellivision-era carts hung every time, the rest loaded fine.

The emulator's receive buffer was sized for the FujiNet mailbox's replies rather than for the much larger frames a cartridge push arrives in, so a block of graphics data that happened to encode badly overran it -- and once that happened the connection could never recover, which is why the bar froze instead of reporting a failure. The buffer is now sized for what it actually carries, and a bad frame is discarded and resynchronized rather than wedging the link.

The keypad window's direction disc now offers every position the real hand controller has. It marks all sixteen sectors instead of eight, resolves a click or drag to the sector it actually landed in -- including the eight half-step positions between the compass directions, which could not be selected at all before -- and lights exactly that one sector.

The highlight itself was wrong in different ways on different systems: pressing the disc lit the whole face rather than a wedge, or lit a wedge three times the width of the sector that produced it. All four frontends now share one definition of the disc's geometry and draw it the same way, so the disc looks and behaves identically wherever you run it.

Cartridges that come as a .bin plus a same-named .cfg memory map now load correctly from the SD host slot. The FujiNet web file manager stored only the first file of an upload and still reported success, so sending a cartridge and its .cfg together left the card holding the .bin alone; the emulator then booted it against a guessed memory map, which for most titles means a black screen, garbage or a hang. Uploads now accept and store every selected file, drag-and-drop included, and name each one in the result.
A cartridge that mounts without its .cfg now says so in the FujiNet log, naming the path it looked for, instead of failing silently.

The debugger's symbol table now persists for the life of the app instead of being thrown away every time the debugger window closes, since loading a game's as1600 symbols is always a manual step taken after FujiNet CONFIG has already booted the cart -- there is no path to auto-load one from. The "Load Symbols..." picker remembers the last folder used. The memory "Address" box and a new "Break at" field accept a symbol name as well as hex. A new Symbols tab lists every loaded symbol, filterable by name, with a click jumping the memory view to that address.

Fixes the debugger's GRAM/GROM card sheet pager: the Prev/Next buttons never appeared at all (a layout bug kept them out of the visible widget tree), so only the first 128 GROM/GRAM cards were ever reachable. Paging now works, shows a "cards N-M of total" range, and clamps at both ends instead of wrapping back to the first page. Fixes the keypad's directional disc lighting the wrong side of the dial (top press lit the bottom wedge, etc.) while still sending the correct direction to the emulator; the highlighted wedge is now correctly oriented and matches the sector that actually produces it.

Boots the larger Intellivision cartridges that previously failed with ERR CODE 3, hangs, or corrupted graphics: cartridge memory maps from a .cfg sidecar are now clamped at end-of-file the way SDK-1600's bin2rom does, cartridges whose ROM occupies the FujiNet mailbox window ($9C00-$9F3F) boot with the mailbox disabled for the session instead of being rejected, .cfg [memattr] cartridge RAM declarations are honored, and 40KB/48KB bare .bin images get sensible default maps. The bundled FujiNet runtime now finds .cfg sidecars on hosts with a path prefix set, verifies the pushed byte count, and aborts cleanly on a short transfer instead of booting partial data. The embedded FujiNet config ROM now names the boot-failure reason on screen.

Fixes audio distortion caused by the emulator's output ring buffer being trimmed too aggressively on hosts with a small audio device quantum, and by underruns playing back stale or uninitialized audio instead of silence. Adds a clickable ECS Keyboard window (F10), the on-screen counterpart to the existing hand-controller keypad, so the ECS's own keyboard can be driven entirely with a mouse.

Adds ECS (Entertainment Computer System) support -- a second controller pair, its own keyboard, and extra sound -- plus Intellivoice speech synthesis and NTSC/PAL video switching, all configurable from a new Settings dialog. ECS and Intellivoice default to Auto, matching each cartridge's own preference.
Updated embedded FujiNet config ROM: the HOST SLOTS screen now has a keypad shortcut that mounts and boots the FujiNet Game Lobby directly, with an on-screen hint showing it's available.
First release of the Intellivision KDE/Qt frontend: the same FujiNet-in-process boot, clickable keypad window, and CP-1610/STIC debugger as the GNOME frontend, built on plain Qt6 Widgets.
